record.original_question: In mushroom billiards and related systems with mixed phase space, how does the boundary between regular and chaotic regions affect escape, including the slowing of survival decay caused by stickiness from marginally unstable periodic orbits and by the regular-chaotic interface itself?

evidence.quote: The decay of the survival probability in the case that the hole is in the chaotic region may be significantly slowed both by stickiness due to marginally unstable periodic orbits, and by the boundary itself.
Open problem 11. Characterise the escape properties of the boundary between regular and chaotic regions in mushroom and similar billiards.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a planar mushroom billiard: the billiard table is the union of a half-disk ("cap") of radius R with a rectangular "stem" of width 2r < 2R attached symmetrically to the diameter of the half-disk, and a point particle moves at unit speed in straight lines inside the table, reflecting elastically at the boundary. The phase space (parametrized by arclength on the boundary and the sine of the angle of incidence) decomposes into a regular component (orbits that remain in the cap forever, those whose chord to the diameter has length greater than 2r) and a chaotic component (orbits that enter the stem). On the interface between these two components there sit families of marginally unstable periodic orbits (MUPOs): periodic orbits in the cap whose chord just touches the corners of the stem, with vanishing Lyapunov exponent. 

Now make the billiard "open" by removing a small hole H from the boundary: a trajectory escapes when it first hits H. Let P(t) denote the survival probability at time t for an initial condition distributed uniformly (with respect to the Liouville measure) on the chaotic component, conditional on not yet having escaped. It is known that when a hole is placed in the chaotic region, the asymptotic decay of P(t) can be slowed both by stickiness produced by MUPOs and by stickiness produced by the regular–chaotic interface itself.

Problem: Give a precise quantitative characterization of the escape properties associated with the boundary between the regular and chaotic regions in mushroom billiards (and analogous mixed-phase-space billiards). In particular, characterize the contribution of the interface (separately from, and together with, the MUPO contribution) to the long-time asymptotics of the survival probability P(t), determining the resulting decay law and how it depends on the geometric parameters (R, r) and on the location and size of the hole.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent literature on mushroom billiards (e.g., works on MUPOs and on tilted-hat / web-like hierarchical mixed phase spaces, as well as 2025 works on quantum chaos in mushroom billiards) continues to investigate stickiness from MUPOs and from the regular–chaotic interface, but no definitive characterization of the escape properties of the regular–chaotic boundary itself appears to have been obtained. The problem appears still open.

status_evidence.title: How sticky is the chaos/order boundary? (Contemporary Mathematics)
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses stickiness of the chaos/order boundary in mushroom billiards and MUPO contributions to survival probability decay.
status_evidence.claim: Surveys mechanisms (MUPO + boundary) slowing decay, but characterization of the boundary's contribution remains a stated open problem.

status_evidence.title: Tilted-hat mushroom billiards: Web-like hierarchical mixed phase space
status_evidence.snippet: Studies hierarchical structure at the regular-chaotic interface in mushroom-type billiards.
status_evidence.claim: Recent work continues to probe interface structure, indicating the escape characterization is not yet settled.

status_evidence.title: Marginally Unstable Periodic Orbits in Semiclassical Mushroom Billiards
status_evidence.snippet: MUPOs lie on the boundary between regular and chaotic regions and dominate stickiness for almost all stem radii.
status_evidence.claim: Identifies MUPO contribution but does not fully characterize the boundary's intrinsic escape properties.
